reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A chronic inflammatory disorder typically affecting young to middle-aged men of Asian descent
Presents with painless subcutaneous nodules or masses in the head and neck, often with regional lymphadenopathy and salivary gland involvement
Marked peripheral blood eosinophilia and strikingly elevated serum IgE are characteristic
Renal involvement, particularly nephrotic syndrome, occurs in a notable minority and should be actively sought
Histology shows lymphoid follicles with germinal centres, dense eosinophilic infiltration with eosinophilic microabscesses, and proliferation of postcapillary venules
Distinct from angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia, which is more superficial and occurs in a different demographic
Benign but frequently relapses after excision; corticosteroids and other systemic immunosuppression are used for extensive or recurrent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Kimura disease is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory condition of unknown cause, possibly reflecting an aberrant T-helper-2 driven allergic or autoimmune response. There is exuberant reactive lymphoid proliferation with well-formed germinal centres accompanied by heavy eosinophil recruitment, elevated IgE, and proliferation of small blood vessels within affected soft tissue and lymph nodes. Cytokines such as interleukin-4 and interleukin-5 are thought to promote the eosinophilia and IgE production. The immune dysregulation may also injure the glomerulus, accounting for the associated nephrotic syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin and T-cell types
Salivary gland tumour or reactive lymphadenopathy
additionalInvestigations: Excisional or core biopsy of the mass for histology showing lymphoid follicles and eosinophilic infiltration
Full blood count with differential documenting peripheral eosinophilia
Serum total IgE, which is characteristically very high
Urinalysis and renal function to detect associated nephrotic syndrome or proteinuria
Cross-sectional imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to define extent and lymph node involvement
Exclusion of parasitic infection and lymphoma where clinically indicated
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or systemic lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma
Constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss requiring exclusion of malignancy
Airway compromise from large head and neck masses
reference.prognosis: Kimura disease is benign and does not undergo malignant transformation, but it is characterised by a chronic, relapsing course with frequent recurrence after excision; associated nephrotic syndrome influences long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Confusing it with angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia, a distinct entity
Failing to check for renal involvement and missing associated nephrotic syndrome
Attributing the mass to malignancy without histological confirmation, or vice versa
Assuming surgical excision is curative when relapse is common
Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient with unexplained eosinophilia and raised IgE
management: Surgical excision of symptomatic head-and-neck nodules or masses as first-line treatment, accepting that recurrence is common
Systemic or intralesional corticosteroids for extensive, recurrent or renal-associated disease
Steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as ciclosporin for relapsing or steroid-dependent disease
Radiotherapy reserved for refractory or repeatedly recurrent lesions
Actively seek and manage renal involvement, particularly nephrotic syndrome, with urinalysis and proteinuria assessment
Monitor peripheral eosinophilia and serum IgE as markers of disease activity
Long-term follow-up given the chronic, relapsing course without malignant transformation
